utterances.text: Miralem carried it with him, but whether he handed it over, I just don't know. As I said, he was the Commander and he was responsible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But as you were there officially, and not privately, who was the records to be turned over to, to the Commander of the Brigade or the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: The Brigade, I guess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, if I understand you well, the Commander of the 333rd Brigade should have this record?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, if it was handed over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, while you were on the shift during those several days, who put the vehicles and names of persons in that book? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I did that on two or three occasions, perhaps, and others. Each one of us did it, depending on who was at the desk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean all of them? You also mean those four of you who were there on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now my last question. Did you ever meet Mr. Kordic personally, anywhere else personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, but it was from a distance. You know, it was when you happened to glimpse Kordic. Well, on one occasion I saw Kordic get out of a vehicle in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it before or after this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: No, before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no more questions. Thank you very much for the patience, and thank you, Witness, for your answers. Cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness AE. You can see me, but because of the protection measures, I can't see you. But I am Goran Mikulicic, a lawyer representing Mr. Mario Cerkez. I shall be very brief. And allow me to ask you only a few questions. Witness AE, you told us you were a member of the 333rd Mountain Brigade, that is reconnaissance sabotage unit. What was the strength of your unit between January and April 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Thirty men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that for a while you were on duty at the checkpoint in Kacuni, but that was not your principal task, the principal task of your platoon, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: It was at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at other periods of time, between January and April, 1993, what was the task of your unit, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Must I answer this question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you think you might be violating a military secret, then you don't have to, but otherwise I think you do. I think you must.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I mean, if you come from Bosnia, you know what was -- what is the task of reconnaissance sabotage platoons. You must know what reconnaissance sabotage units did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not from Bosnia, nor are the honourable members of the Court from Bosnia, so will you please tell us what this term means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Well, I think that the name itself is self-telling, is telling enough. It is reconnaissance and sabotage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I may be, therefore, properly guessing, but I am not a professional. The task of this platoon is to make rounds of the area, which is within the area of responsibility of the Brigade it belongs to, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if during this period of time that we are referring to, that is between January and April, 1993, what was the strength of the 333rd Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You wouldn't know even the approximate number. I'm not asking you the exact number of men, but you wouldn't have the approximate strength?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Well, it had three battalions, plus units attached to the Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be around 1,400 men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Well, about 500 or 600 men less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AE, you said that you did rounds of the area. Could you tell us, what positions did the 333rd Mountain Brigade hold in the municipality of Busovaca? Again, roughly which locations would that be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Around Busovaca, the 333rd, plus a part of the 7th Muslim. Sead Sljivar was their Commander and it had its headquarters in Kacuni and was an autonomous unit, it wasn't part of the Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And the 333rd, and you were its member, did it hold some positions in the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it hold some positions in the Novi Travnik municipality or Travnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Witness AE, you're claiming that your Brigade, the 333rd Mountain Brigade, held positions only in the territory of Busovaca municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Witness AE, do you know Mr. Mario Cerkez? Have you ever seen him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A couple of matters arising. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you connect the killing of Delija to the incident at the checkpoint that had happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May it please the Court. I object to that question. It would be pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It has to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's probably right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With respect, no. The position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I don't think it's going to help us to know his thought processes on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, he's been challenged as to the identification of the person, and one's thought processes can, indeed, highlight or otherwise diminish a recollection at the time. If something is thought to be significant, it may well be in your memory and stay in your memory from then on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's fairly obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on to the only other point I want to raise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 24th of January incident where one person was killed, how many vehicles altogether were involved? How many vehicles arrived at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: On the 24th of January?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: One vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people in that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Two men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the vehicle itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: A Zolja was fired at it. The vehicle was there, but a dead man was in it, the driver, and I've already said twice that there was no other person in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other man left on foot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there firing at your checkpoint by the people in the car or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. I said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I need to confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness AE, that concludes your evidence and you are now released. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While the courtroom is being prepared for the departure of this particular Witness, Mr. Lopez-Terres is taking the next Witness and there's an application for protection in respect of that witness, and I'll ask Mr. Lopez-Terres to deal with it and I shall withdraw briefly. The third Witness, Mr. Beese, is here today. If possible, it would be nice for him to be released this afternoon so that he can fly back this evening. I may have one other thing to say about him before lunchtime, but I'll hand it over to Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have just been handed the application, Mr. Lopez-Terres. It's an application relating to pseudonym and face distortion, and we can see in paragraph 2 of the application the reason that it's made, due to his current residence, really. I turn to the Defence. Is there any objection to this application?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Not from Mr. Kordic's Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll grant the application and the terms outlined.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The pseudonym for this Witness will be Witness AF.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the Witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could the usher show the Witness a document with his name written on it so that he can recognise it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, the Witness nodded his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, would it be possible for this hearing to have a private session to begin with, to verify certain identification issues with the Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the village where you are living, the village of Tulica to which you returned recently, is a village that had about 78 houses and a population of about 350 in 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This population was exclusively of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have provided to our investigators a sketch indicating the position of those houses and the names of the families living in them, and I should like that document to be shown to you as you will be referring to it as we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are several documents that are going to be used during the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the document be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AF, do you recognise this sketch, with the houses indicated, as the one that you provided to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, if the witness is going to refer to it, the interpreters are asking that it goes on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the reservation that the name of the witness appears on the document. It has been signed by the witness at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let us deal with it without putting it on the ELMO, but do it as quickly as you can, please, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document consists of two pages. On one part is the lower part of the village and, on the other part, the upper part of the village; is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. Because of the size of the paper, I couldn't draw it all on one sheet of paper, so I had to continue on to the next sheet, which is in fact one and the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also provided a list of the owners of those houses, a list attached to this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, with the numbers indicated of the owners of the houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this document is Z2104.3. Witness, the village of Tulica is situated about 16 kilometres from Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the course of your testimony you are going to refer to several localities, or places, and I should like to show you another document so that the Chamber can check the geographic area in which Tulica is situated. So could it be shown to the witness, a map marked Z1891.2. Very well. You have told us that the village of Tulica was a village inhabited exclusively by Muslims, situated south of Kiseljak. This village was surrounded partly by almost exclusively Croat villages, such as Azapovici, Homolj, Kulijes, Lepenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were also a few hamlets inhabited by Serbs near Tulica, and those were Rudnik and Ostrik. In the course of 1992, and especially in June, 1992, after the outbreak of the war with the Serbs, the area of Tulica found itself on the front line with the Serbs, and the villages were occasionally shelled by Serb artillery; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. From Vela, Vocnjak, and Cilena, it is not marked on the map. It is to the right of the map, the positions from where the firing came. Then also Bare, the municipality of Hadzici, and we also said that Vocnjak is not marked on this map. Vela, Rudnik and Ostrik also. Rudnik, Ostrik, those are Serb positions there. At Ostrik, that was where the front line was. The Serb front lines were at Ostrik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To complete the discussion regarding localities, I should like to show you a final document which indicates the front lines between the different combatants, and this is Exhibit Z2097. Can you see Tulica on this map, witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Tulica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the very edge where the areas of responsibility of Republika Srpska and the BiH Army meet, does this correspond to the reality as you knew it in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, it does correspond to the real situation. Tulica is here, within the area under the control of the HVO [indicates]. The Army of Republika Srpska looking towards Kiseljak to the right, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were at Koscan, and also around Bihac, down here. Those were the areas under the control of the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Due to the hostilities with the Serbs and the shelling, some women and children of the village left Tulica, and they left to go to Slovenia for a while?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992, after the first heavy shelling, the women and children fled to Slovenia. Four months later they returned, because of the conditions they were provided in collective shelters in Slovenia and because of the separation of families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we say that in June, 1993, the population of the village, which used to be 350, was reduced to about 250?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. The people who had family members in Germany, Austria or Sweden, went from Slovenia to those countries, whereas the others, who didn't have people abroad, returned. So about 250 were there on the 12th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among men of military age in the village, some had left the village to be deployed in other areas under BiH Army control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, the younger, able-bodied men left to join the BiH Army and other units around Sarajevo, Pazarici, Koscan, and other units that had been formed at that time. So that they would occasionally come home on leave, until the 12th of June, 1993, when the village was attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any military units or military installations in the village of Tulica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: There were absolutely no military units in Tulica, except for the soldiers who would come occasionally on leave from their units. There were no military units in the village. It was inhabited by exclusively civilian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of weapons did the villagers have in their possession?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: They had only personal weapons and hunting weapons; hunting rifles and pistols with appropriate permits to carry such weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was no artillery piece or a heavy weapon of a high calibre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: No, there was never any artillery pieces. There were only a few automatic rifles, two or three of them, which the reservists had when the police was divided up, and then the guards, village guards, were given these hunting weapons and pistols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated, on the map a moment ago, where the front lines were between the three belligerent parties. As regards the Serbs and the HVO soldiers in the area, were you able to note that there was an agreement between these two factions and relatively friendly relations between them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, because they were all in one line. For instance, at Kobiljaca were the Serbs; Batalovo Brdo, again Serbs; the Pljesevac hill was held by Croats; Ravne, Croats; Ostrik, Serbs. All this is in a straight line. And they co-operated. And from Kobiljaca, this is the meeting point of three municipalities: Kiseljak, Ilidza, and Hadzici, and then a border line was cut through the woods of some 10 metres across the hill of Pljesevac towards Kobiljaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you know, the Serbs and the HVO soldiers in the area, did they ever fight against one another?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Never in that area, because they visited one another across the front lines, because they were in contact with each other, and they even built joint positions. The Croats participated in the transportation of materials along paths where it was difficult to pass, and there was a lot of smuggling of cigarettes and alcohol and other products, and they held positions jointly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, could one say that there was a non-aggression pact between the Croats and the Serbs of the region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: We are not aware of any kind of pact, but judging by this behaviour, we believed that there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 12th of June, 1993, Witness, it was a Saturday, just before 12, the village was shelled for more than three hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. The first shell fell on the village of Tulica, on the 12th of June, 1993, on a Saturday, at about ten to 12 in the morning. That was when the first shell was fired. Then, some ten minutes later, heavy shelling started from all artillery pieces on the village of Tulica, and this went on for three and a half hours non-stop. This was very heavy shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of your experience, you were able to establish the calibre of these pieces and especially the 120-, 82-, and 60-millimetre shells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. In view of the fact that when Serbs were attacking positions at Koscan, those shells would fly over our village. So judging by the detonations, since we were in the village for some time until the 12th of June, we could recognise the calibre of the weapons used to shell the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your military service, you gained some experience yourself regarding the calibre of guns and shells.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. I served in the former Yugoslav People's Army; I was in the transportation service, a driver, so that I knew howitzers. For instance, of 122-, 155-millimetres, I would transport them to positions where military exercises were being held, shooting exercises, using this kind of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the shelling you are telling us about took place at the end of the morning on the 12th of June, 1993, and there was no doubt in your mind that it came from Serb positions in the area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, most probably from Serb positions. This may have been a kind of trick so that we would believe that the Serbs were attacking. Later on we heard that the Serbs had been paid to shell the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those Serb positions that you are referring to are those that you showed us on the map a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Bare, Batolovo Brdo, Vela, Rudnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you also had information that it was the HVO that had participated in the shelling from their positions at Cubren that they also had shelled.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I couldn't notice this in view of the position I was in at the time, because of these numerous detonations, but I heard this from my neighbours who were closer by, in Lepenica, and they said that some of the fire had come from above Brkovici, the hill of Cubren, that mortar shells had been fired from those mortar positions there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until that day, you experienced only artillery attacks, and by that time, there were no infantry attacks, were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: No. At that moment, we did not expect them, although we were not quite clear because this was the first time that it was happening in a year, to have such heavy shelling which was destroying the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of those three or three and a half hours of shelling, you saw the soldiers enter the village, and these soldiers were coming from different directions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, soldiers were arriving from Ban Brdo, that is, from Cuprija, they were accommodated there, and then they were deployed from the hill of Ostrik, or, rather, below Ostrik, and then down in six groups, as the village is 1.2 kilometres long. So they entered in about some six or seven groups, the soldiers entered the village after the shelling and covered, with their infantry, the whole of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The villagers, at the beginning of this attack, they thought that this was a Serb attack, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. Since the men were taking shelter during the shelling in that house, in this first house, one could hear the house cracking because fire was put to them, and I thought it was the shelling which set the house on fire. However, he ran to that house with the owner of the house to try to put the fire out. However, they came across a group of some eight or ten soldiers, that is what they told us, wearing black uniforms, with masks over their faces, who shouted "Halt," to stop and to surrender. However, this man who had just left me, he managed to escape and the owner, Safet Katkic, the owner of that house which was burning, which was the closest to Ostrik, to Serb positions, he was arrested and killed later on. We were told, in view of the vicinity or the closeness of Serb positions, he said, "Well, Chetniks have entered the village and are torching the village, so get away. You must all seek shelter."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you realised subsequently that those were HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. After a while, after we had pulled out from the village at the place where I had found refuge, I was controlling a side from Donji Azapovici, that is, from the locality of Glavica and Donji Azapovici, where trenches had been dug, and there I saw a group of soldiers, ten soldiers, approaching the lower part of Tulica. Then it dawned upon me that it was an HVO attack because there were no Serb soldiers at that particular place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the attack, before we come to various stages of it which you witnessed, you went back to your house, and your brother also, to get your weapons. Could you please tell us, what kind of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, where we were sheltering, as my house was quite nearby, I collected my personal weapons, all that we had, that is, my brother and I, and we went to relatives and we collected those -- we picked up those weapons. Some 30 metres from our house is a mill, a water mill, and four of us got there and we split into two groups, two and two, in order to try to get out to an open area, to a clearing, where the soldiers could see us. They saw my relative and me and opened fire on us. However, neither of us was hit and we made it to the woods, and from there we observed what was going on in Tulica and further developments; that is, the torching and all the rest, the arrest of people, and then killing later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, we shall come to that a bit later. But those weapons, those weapons which you and your brother picked up, did you have an opportunity to use them that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes -- no, no. No, we did not use any of them because it would have meant an additional burden because people would suffer more. Had anyone used any weapon, then the butchery might have been even worse than it actually was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have just told us, you commented that soldiers fired at houses with incendiaries, didn't they? And you saw Muhamed Huseinovic's stable which was also torched.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: There are some four or five houses near the forest, a bit away from the village, so perhaps they did not dare because somebody might have fired from the forest or something. So they dared not approach those houses and set fire to them themselves, and they rather used incendiaries. Muhamed Huseinovic's stable was thus put on fire and a cow and a calf burnt in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the attack, you could hear soldiers singing and shouting insults.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. All the time as they were torching in the upper part of the village, they were singing because they had no reason to fear any resistance of the villagers, because they had arrested everybody and separated men from women and children. So they were singing, and they were singing, "The two brothers of us who are both waging war. Do not cry, Mother, if we get killed," and they also insulted particularly -- particularly hurling insults at the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, saying, "Balijas, you will remember us" and similar insults.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From that place where you were sheltering with your brother in the forest, you were able to see what was going on in the vicinity of the cemetery and in the lower part of the village, and you could see soldiers who were breaking into houses and forcing the villagers to get out, and then making the move towards the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. So during the torching, at the same time, they were also arresting people who were there after the shelling, the people who were working in the fields, because it was the 12th of June, a very fine summer day, sunny. So people were working in the fields, and after the shelling, those people started to go home and there they were arrested. Those people who were in the village during the shelling could not leave the village because of the intensity of the shelling. So they were arresting all whom were alive, whom they could find, and they were taken to the cemetery, and by the cemetery, they separated women and children and took them down the road, I could not see where; I saw where the women were about half an hour later. And now I could see the cemetery where men were being rounded up from the upper and the lower part of the village and brought there, next to the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you saw what happened to the group of men. As for women, some of them, later on, you told us what happened to them. Could you please tell us, in a few words, what you saw.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. People were brought to this cemetery and were lined up. From the place where I was, they had their backs to me. That is how they were turned so they could not see what was happening behind their backs. So that was next to Huseinovic's house. So some 35 of them were lined up, and then they would be taken out and some would be singled out from that group of 35 who had their backs to me, and ill-treatment started, that is, physical harassment began, next to the cemetery. They took out Zijad Huseinovic, Aziz Huseinovic, Casim Huseinovic, Safet Haskic, Refik Huseinovic, Ahmed Bajraktarevic, and Mufid Tulic. That is all those who were killed right next to the cemetery and who had been taken out of that line. They were singled out from that line, ill-treated, and then killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of them were battered before they were killed on the spot; that is what happened to Kasim Huseinovic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, Kasim Huseinovic, that man was subjected to the worst harassment of all of them, because they used rifle butts. There was three soldiers and then more soldiers in black uniforms joined them to beat him with their rifle butts, in the chest, on the head. He fell down on the road, then they would kick him and then again force him to stand up. And so in that group between them he experienced the worst ill-treatment of all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aziz Huseinovic, whom you mentioned before, he was executed. He was also wounded in the leg, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, Aziz was first singled out. And a soldier in a baseball cap with this yellow, what you call it, this shield for some protection, he fired at his leg and wounded him. And I saw Aziz fall down on one leg and then sat on the grass and took his T-shirt to bind the wound, to stop the bleeding. After that, this soldier made a few steps away from Aziz, fired at him and killed him right there next to the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also saw some other men, you gave us their name, being forced to run down a slope, which was near the cemetery, and then they were hit as they were running down that slope.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, quite. It is a clearing which from the cemetery you run down to a stream, and there was grass about half a metre tall. And there they took Safet Katkic, Refik Huseinovic and, in the same way, all of them, Aziz and what's his name, Mufid Tulic, Ahmed Bajraktarevic, and all in the same way. They would take out men, tell them to go down that slope, the man starts down it, and they fire at the back. And then the man rolls down that slope because it was quite a steep slope. And so four of them were killed in an identical way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described to us the men who killed those men. You particularly remember that one of them was wearing a black leather jacket, and whose nickname was Pijuk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, we heard that later, after those -- after those were killed, the rest of the arrested were taken to the barracks at Kiseljak, and they were exchanged three days later, and for ten of them. And they told us, because those guys who were arrested, they knew them. They used to socialise before the war in Kiseljak. And they knew Pijuk and the nickname -- somebody who was nicknamed Crnogorac and Montenegrin. And they told us that it was these men. And they were the ones who also killed those four. So he was wearing a black leather jacket, black uniform, sleeveless jacket, and he also had a stocking over his head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the two other soldiers, the two other soldiers who participated in this, you also mentioned them, and you said their nicknames were Crnogorac and Firga, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, those who were in the barracks and were subsequently changed, they recognised them and they told us at the place where they were taken -- they were taken to the place where they had been executed and they recognised them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those soldiers came from Kiseljak, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: So all these soldiers -- well, it depended on the place where who was who. I told you all the villages were scattered, but they knew some people, and they were all from Lepenica, from Brnjaci, from Kiseljak, Gromiljak. That is, they all came from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what special unit did those men belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. They were Maturice and Apostoli, the so-called strike units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the attack, there were not only the soldiers in black uniforms, there were also wearing camouflage uniforms, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, some were wearing camouflage uniforms. And those must have been the security around the village, in view of the closeness of HVO positions. And down there some soldiers were standing guard. But after the torching and other things like that, then a plunder took place, and those in camouflage uniforms were taking away household appliances and all the rest of the valuable things. They brought in trucks and they took it all out from the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally see those scenes of plunder?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, I saw a few cars. There were a few cars, and a number of lorries, and various household appliances were loaded onto them and other things; how they were loaded onto them and then driven away to Lepenica, or even carts, wheel carts, for instance, that the villagers in Tulica had. They would load a TV set and then similar things, video recorders and such like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This looting, was it done by HVO soldiers or by civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: HVO soldiers. Only HVO soldiers. There were no civilians. It used to be a Bosniak village, so there were no other people there. After we had left, we do not know what was going on there and what happened there. I don't know after we fled, and that was two or three days later, we do not know what came to pass with other people or other things, other property that had stayed in the houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you personally witnessed the death of seven villagers, and you were told also that an eighth villager was killed, and you heard about the circumstances under which that had happened. And you had been told that by women from the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. After we left the village of Tulica, we moved to Bukovica with a Muslim majority, and most of the people had left the village of Tulica and got there. And there, because many were coming there from other places, and women -- Fata Bajraktarevic's wife, Safija Bajraktarevic and other women, told me that in front of Arif's house, or rather, where Arif Bajraktarevic used to have his shop, that that was where women had -- had met. And Salko Bajraktarevic had come there, and he was 65 to 70 years of age, and he came there where those women were rounded up, and said, "Come on, men, what are you doing to us?" And they told him, "Shut your mouth, older man, or we will kill you." And he told them, "Well, kill me, if I've wronged you in any way." And this man, that is this HVO soldier in a black uniform, sleeveless, that is a sleeveless leather, black leather jacket, he simply turned his rifle around and fired at the old man and killed him right in front of all those women. And it subsequently turned out that he was the first one to have been killed in the village of Tulica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are talking about Mr. Salko Bajraktarevic; is that so? Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those same women, those women that you just mentioned, and we already asked you about them, and you told us what had happened in front of Salko Bajraktarevic's house, that they were forced to turn over their belongings to soldiers, to HVO soldiers. Arif Bajraktarevic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Quite. Yes. The women said those soldiers spread something on the ground, and women who were detained there, who were there, they said all that they had made of gold, that is rings or chains, whatever they had valuable, that they should take it off and throw it onto that rag, onto that cloth that was spread onto the ground. And the women did that, and were taken to Dzemal Huseinovic's house in the village, and locked there. They could not come out until everything else was going on in the village, until the end of the attack on the village. After that, they were released and then they sought refuge elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, among those eight men who were killed on that day, there were also three women who were killed during the attack on the village, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, but later on, when we had already fled, we were told that Safija Tulic, about 70 years old, that she was burnt alive in her house. Fatima Bajraktarevic, and to this day we do not know what her fate is, she headed off toward Kulijes, and no trace of her. And Sifa Tulic, who also headed off towards Kulijes, she was hit from a distance, and those who were nearer could hear. They said they could hear how she moaned and cried for a long time. And, in all likelihood, she must have been hit, and she bled to death. And she was found later on in a field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who survived the attack were taken to the barracks in Kiseljak, you told us. And there was a truck which waited there to take them to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, I went to -- across to the other part of the forest, to see what was going on. And they were in front of Ibrahim Jahic's house. There was a truck, a two tonne truck belonging to the public amenity company in Kiseljak. It was waiting there, and other men were waiting there, some 25 of them altogether. And they were put onto that truck and taken first to Lepenica and then to Kiseljak, to the Kiseljak barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned Ibrahim Jahic. Could you tell us what happened to that particular individual?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Ibrahim Jahic was arrested there by that house, together with all the others; was taken towards Lepenica in the truck. However, a white Golf with HVO soldiers, I could see how he discarded something out, threw away something from the truck. That man had a lot of money, and that they thought that he'd thrown away that money into the wheat field. And in Lepenica they took Ibrahim Jahic from the truck, ill-treated him there in Lepenica, I mean physically ill-treated him, and put him into that vehicle and turned back to the village of Tulica, and there has been no trace of him ever since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any information that Mr. Jahic was killed while he was digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, seven days later all the others were exchanged, I mean the Tulica villages. During that time there was absolutely no trace of Ibrahim Jahic amongst them, that is in the barracks, nor had anybody set eyes on him. But after a while we learnt through an individual that Ibrahim Jahic had been taken to dig. And according to them, in mektef, that is the religious object in Svinjarevo, they found Ibrahim Jahic with documentation in his pocket and his body was decomposing by that time. And that soldier ordered others who were digging to dig their grave two metres from the mektef, and to bury him there. And that is what they did. And when we learnt that, we asked for his exhumation, to give him a proper burial together with others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I conclude, Witness AF, I should like to show you a set of photographs, Z2104. Will you please have a look at this album. Could you please tell us if these photographs show the houses destroyed in Tulica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. The upper part of the village was damaged, the upper part of the village of Tulica. That was set on fire. And the lower part. And these are mostly newer houses, new development, only Zifet Huseinovic's house was set on fire, and therefore destroyed. And the last shells that hit the village, that fell that day, Saban Bajraktarevic -- hit Saban Bajraktarevic's house. So the houses in the lower part of Tulica, then Croat -- Croat refugees from Vares then moved into those houses which had remained intact in the lower part of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, among these photographs, is there a photograph of that religious object that you mentioned, the mektef?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. Just a moment. Well, this is the picture of mektef.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, can I just be sure about this. Is it the Prosecution case that 11 people were killed in this attack, eight men and three women? That appears to be the evidence, but I want to make sure that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Death certificates were produced together with the Tulica file, Tulica dossier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now till half past 2 for cross-examination then. Witness AF, don't speak to anybody, please, during the adjournment about your evidence, and don't let anybody speak to you about it until it's over. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.04 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Sayers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness AF. My name is Stephen Sayers; I'm one of the attorneys representing Dario Kordic. I have about ten minutes of questions for you, sir. First, in connection with the artillery fire that you identified on the early afternoon, I believe you said, of the 12th of June, 1993, you said it came from Serb positions; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also observed that you had "heard" that the Serbs had somehow been paid to shell your village; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. We had the report that it had been paid for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any documentation that verified those reports, receipts or things of that variety, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: No. I wasn't in a position to have access to any kind of documents of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, sir. It's true, is it not, that you never heard any Serb Artillery Commander or soldier contend that the Serb artillery had, in fact, been hired, if you like, by the Croats or the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Individuals were saying that, and these individuals were next to Kobiljaca whose neighbours were Serbs. They heard from a Serb neighbour that this had been paid for, for Tulica to be shelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you yourself, Witness AF, you yourself never heard anything of that variety from any Serb soldier or, for that matter, any HVO soldier; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: We didn't hear it from any Serb soldier because we had no contact, nor did we dare to have any contact because the Army was nearby, and the BH Army was fighting the Serb aggressor. So it was not possible to get in touch with any Serb soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You never heard from any HVO soldier that monies had been paid to the Serbs to fire artillery shells or mortar shells onto your village; isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: We couldn't because after the attack we never met with Croatian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, sir. All I'm saying is your information on that really comes from the rumour mill in the villages that were in the area of Tulica; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: From rumours, yes, but in view of the co-operation they had, that is, the HVO soldiers and the Serb soldiers, in the area, in this part of the territory, one could infer that there was truth in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, you were shown a series of photographs by the Prosecution, and you identified these as pictures of houses in Tulica. Do you know who took these photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's true, equally, that you don't know when these photographs were taken; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There appears to be Agency for Information and Documentation stamps, Muslim Intelligence Agency stamps on the top left-hand corner and the top right-hand corner of each of these. Do you know who put these stamps on here, sir, these AID stamps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with the songs that you heard the soldiers who were attacking Tulica singing, you said in your statement that some Serb name was being shouted and that this name probably was the name of the soldier who was actually shouting the dire threats. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: In view of the fact that they had entered through the positions of the Serb Army and they would mention a name, this was a trick to the effect, "You will see what so and so is," and all this was meant to give the impression that the Serbs were attacking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's your conclusion, correct, looking back on the events eight years ago -- seven years ago; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the testimony that you gave in connection with the blanket that was placed on the ground and the valuables that were required to be placed upon that blanket, that testimony is derived from things that you were told by other people; isn't that correct? You didn't actually see the event yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I didn't see the event because of the position where I was, I couldn't see it. But later on, when we were in exile, all the women who were there confirmed this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, Witness AF. The only point that I'm making is that your testimony on that subject is really derived from what you were told, not what you saw or heard yourself; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, quite correct. I didn't see that. I couldn't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also gave some testimony about observing people you say were shot by soldiers. How far away from the actual scene where those killings were taking place were you, 200 metres, 300 metres, further than that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: As the crow flies, and in view of the valley beneath, it is about 150 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in connection with the testimony that you gave relating to the killing of Salko Bajraktarevic -- please forgive my pronunciation -- you did not actually see that yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: No, I didn't because you cannot walk around in a leisurely manner when the HVO had covered the whole village with infantry, and as this house is in the lower part of the village, I couldn't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I take your point precisely, but the only point that I'm trying to establish is that your testimony regarding Mr. Bajraktarevic's killing is based upon what other people told you; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with the three ladies that you have identified as having been killed or having been presumptively killed, with respect to Fatima Bajraktarevic, you really do not know any facts about what happened to her at all, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I don't know, but in view of the people who went to the Croatian settlement of Kulis, they were either wounded or killed, and that woman went in that direction, and all trace of her was lost. And to this day nobody knows what happened to her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in connection with the death of Sifa Tulic, you weren't actually there when the events happened? You didn't see them yourself, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it. It is on the other side of me, close to the Croatian settlement of Kulis. It is on the other side. But other villagers heard the screaming for some time. And afterwards they found her. She had been wounded in the legs and she probably bled to death.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, could you speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sorry. This is a little awkward, being the number three man here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the point I am making with you, Witness AF, is that what you know about the circumstances under which Sifa Tulic died, your knowledge of that is derived from what you were told by other people who were actually there, or may have heard from people who were there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. When we were in exile, on the second day, the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. My next to last question is concerned with the testimony that you gave relating to Ibrahim Jahic. This is the gentleman who was taken away from Tulica and transported north. And you do not yourself know from your own personal knowledge what happened to him? Your information or conclusions relating to what happened to him are really based upon what other people told you; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: I actually found the information about that man, and I can tell you the name who buried him, Enver Fazlibasic. He was in captivity, held by the HVO in Kiseljak. And he was also taken to dig trenches, facing the positions in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I understand, Witness AF, but the only point I am making is that what you know about what supposedly happened to Mr. Jahic, is things that you were told by other people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then my final question to you, sir, is after you were able to leave Tulica, after witnessing the events that you've testified about, you actually made your way to the Croat village of Josipovici, and found shelter with a Croat friend of yours who lived there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: At first, when we still didn't know exactly who had attacked the village, we fled, and because of the life we used to have, we had many friends there. And we headed towards a Croatian village and where our families had gone to. But a smaller number of families went there. And people took shelter there, while the shooting and torching went on. And that is where I found my family. And from there, there were some 70 or 80 of us, women, children and men, we headed on to seek refuge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you asked for help from your Croat neighbours, and that help was given; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: We didn't ask for help, but my father --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you. The point is that you stayed with some Croatians; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's the end of the questions that I would have for the Witness. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few points of clarification from the Witness. Excuse me, I hadn't heard that Mr. Mikulicic was on his feet. However, as his client has not been charged for the events in Tulica, I thought he would not have any cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is precisely so, as my learned friend has said, the Defence has no questions, as these are events for which my client has not been charged. Re-examined by Mr. Lopez-Terres:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness AF, regarding this attack, artillery attack coming from the Serbs sector, you said that you personally have no proof that agreements had been reached between the HVO and the Serbs for the village to be attacked by the Serbs, after being paid for it by the HVO. But, you personally did see and hear that the firing at the village, on the 12th of June, 1993, came mostly from positions where artillery pieces of the Serbs were situated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Because we spent a year in the village, and from those same positions, positions of the BiH Army were shelled. And these shells flew over our village. Every time an artillery piece fired from those positions, we could hear it in the village where we were living and working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A second point linked to this attack. Is there any doubt in your mind, witness, that the attacks against the village were committed by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: There were no Serbs, absolutely. It was the HVO troops that attacked the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last point regarding the visit you made to a Croatian friend who took you in. I am not asking you to give us the name of that person, but could you quickly and briefly tell us what you heard and saw while you were staying with that friend, when a local HVO Commander came to visit that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AE
utterances.text: Yes. When I found my family, this Croat told me to get into the house as quickly as possible. I did. I took off my shoes in front of the door. The shoes were immediately carried in after me. As soon as I had sat down, a Yugo 45 car, a grey coloured car, arrived. A local Commander was there, Kapetanovic and someone known as Macan, whose name I do not know. He was the local Commander there, together with Zuna, Vlatko Trogrlic. So that this was about five or six metres from the window. And I heard this Croat, who was our host, who went out immediately. And he was asked whether there were any villagers there, any local people from Tulica in his house. He said there were not. There were none. However, this neighbour and relative joined in the conversation; he's a son-in-law. He interrupted this conversation with this Croat, whose house we were in. He said, "What kind of an army are you, when you are shooting at women and children?" And he said, "We are not shooting. We are only shooting those who are resisting." Then this man called Pivac, known as Pivac, said that he can say what he likes, but he cannot deny what this man himself had seen with his own eyes. Then this man got angry, switched on his engine and left in his car towards Lepenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness AF, that concludes your evidence here. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we turn to the next witness, can I invite the Chamber to look at the summary of Mr. Beese's evidence that you should, I think, have from previous occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The ruling that the Chamber has given is in respect of paragraph 5(b). I am going to ask the Chamber to reconsider the ruling, in light of a particular matter, to deal with simply 5(c). In addition, 5(c) relates to a meeting that the witness had with Kordic on the 5th of May, and the Chamber will remember from the material upon which the witness relies, that he's one of the witnesses, one of the, I think, comparatively small number of witnesses who has and speaks from literally contemporaneous notes. And if you look a couple of pages on in the summary, you'll see the other way around, the very detailed notes of the meeting he had with Kordic on the 5th of May. Now, you will remember the shape of the argument --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are we in open session or -- we are. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court will remember the shape of the argument about Mr. Beese's evidence generally, and the fact that it was in two different types, material that was new, and material that was commentary and general conclusions, which the Chamber excluded. And the Chamber may recall that His Honour Judge Bennouna interrupted my argument at one stage and said, "Well, are you telling me that in relation to the 28th of April, this is new matter?" I said that I was. And then the Chamber conferred and said, "Well, you can have the new matter," which was paragraph 5(b). Now, as to paragraph 5(c), what had been said by Mr. Sayers was that the meeting on the 5th of May was one at which Witness AA had already -- was also in attendance. That can be found on page 13,255, where he said, apparently, Witness AA was present at that meeting. Now, I wasn't in a position then to check on that detail, and assume that what he said was accurate. In fact, as I've confirmed with the witness this morning, the meeting on the 5th of May was a meeting involving three European Community Ambassadors, so those are simply not witnesses we have called, or have ever been anywhere near calling, saving the most exceptional circumstances. As the Chamber already knows, witnesses at that grade don't come in. One or two may have done, but it's very much the exception. And he, the witness, was the only other person present at that meeting, apart from an interpreter. It's also the case that he, simply having introduced the ambassadors, sat there and talked. The contemporaneous notes which I've already drawn to your attention, they are very detailed and simply record what was being said. On the 5th of May, we have had evidence of another meeting that was between Kordic and the witness Payam Akhavan, and the Chamber will recall that there was substantial cross-examination of the general quality and character of Akhavan's evidence generally, and I don't know -- I haven't been able to find the specific challenge to what was said on the 5th of May -- but the Chamber may think that this is an extremely helpful piece of evidence, as accurate as it can conceivably be, assuming the witness is truthful about making contemporaneous notes, and the Chamber will see under 5(c) various things said by the defendant Kordic, and in particular what he said, at Roman VI, VII, and VIII, about Ahmici. It was a misunderstanding when it was suggested that Witness AA was present at the meeting, and these things do happen, but we all proceeded on the basis that that might be correct, it not having been checked and verified, and, of course, this meeting does fall into exactly the same category as the piece of additional evidence that the witness can give in relation to the 28th of April meeting, where, indeed, Witness AA was present but where Witness AA was unable to give us the detail that this witness can. So that 5(c), which won't take very long to adduce and, indeed, may not be challenged, 5(c) falls in the same category of new material of a high quality, and I'd ask to be given leave to lead it. I notified my friend Mr. Stein this morning that it was my intention to do so, to seek your leave to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we've considered the matter. We are being asked, effectively, to change our ruling, it being said that it was made under a misapprehension; however, I remember quite well that we were reluctant to make the ruling at all and it was only when it was pointed out that this was an important issue on which you would be entitled to call evidence in rebuttal anyway, that we decided to allow the evidence in. So the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases. But as I explained, the matter proceeded on a misunderstanding, not entirely of my creation. May the witness come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course you can call some evidence about who he is and why he was there and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May it please the Court. I should always sit down a winner, but I must say that there was no misrepresentation by Mr. Sayers. The record is quite clear what he is referring to and, indeed, the notes, contemporaneous notes, at the first paragraph are consistent with that interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are not going to adjudicate on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat, Mr. Beese.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: Christopher David Beese.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your career, Mr. Beese, was in the army between 1973 and 1977; in insurance, I think, for the next three years; in the Oman Army from 1982 to 1987; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In security from 1988 to 1992, and working for the ECMM between January and August of 1993.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Initially, were you stationed in Siroki Brijeg, Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the head of the coordination centre in Mostar from February or March and until about April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then become the Deputy Head of the Regional Centre in Zenica, reporting to Ambassador Thebault in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're here, in fact, for one piece of evidence only, and it relates to an event on the 28th of April of 1993. Do you have some notes in relation to that event?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have them with you? If you would like to open them. We have a page which is headed "Zenica 28/4".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When you say "we," who has it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I trust Your Honour has it. I'd been referring a little earlier to the pages at the back of the summary, and I hope that if you turn to the back of the summary, you will find --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- some handwritten documents, as well as some typed documents. It's the first of the handwritten documents, and the witness has the original of it before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, tell us a little bit about this event, although there's only one detail of it that we particularly want from you, but just to get the setting. Where was this meeting that is, as we can see, covered by your note of the 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: In the Hotel International in central Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was present?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: The purpose of the meeting was to hold a discussion between Generals Sefer Halilovic and Milivoj Petkovic, chaired by Ambassador Jean-Pierre Thebault; to discuss activity in connection with the ceasefire agreements that the two parties, the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims, had signed; to discuss the following day's agenda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The setting for this meeting, why were you meeting these people and why do you refer to it, as it were, as "the following day's agenda"?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: Following a meeting in Zagreb between President Tudjman of Croatia and President Ilija Izetbegovic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and their respective Generals, Petkovic and Halilovic, there was an agreement to effect ceasefires throughout Bosnia and to reinstitute freedom of movement and to set up a joint military headquarters, staffed by Officers of the two respective parties. The purpose of the meeting was to discuss how the two military commanders would move about the area the following day; to meet dignitaries, important persons, military, in the region; to ensure that the combatants of each side fully understood the nature of this agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were number two to Ambassador Thebault at this time.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: I had recently arrived from Mostar at Jean-Pierre Thebault's request to take on responsibility as his new Deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The notes that we see, when were they made in relation to matters that were happening or being discussed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: They were made at the time by me as the meeting took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the meeting, who was doing the speaking from your side, you or Ambassador Thebault?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: At this stage, Ambassador Thebault was chairing the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were in a position --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: As an observer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- to listen and observe. We can briskly, then, go through the first half of the meeting. Halilovic says in summary that the Vitez agreement was not violated.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic was explaining that he'd given the orders for the ceasefire to take effect. There was some discussion between the two Commanders as to whether the ceasefires they had agreed were, in fact, taking place. General Petkovic was uncertain that General Halilovic had passed all the orders to his subordinates and quoted specifically that there was still conflict around Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And we see that in "Busovaca tells a different story"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: Correct. While Sefer Halilovic said that he had passed the orders so that he was fully compliant with the ceasefire agreement, General Petkovic differed and said that events in Busovaca told a different story, that, therefore, perhaps General Halilovic had not passed the orders to all his troops for a ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We then see an entry that, I think, has Thebault's name beside it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you interpret that for us?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, while we were discussing the relative merits of each other's ceasefire arrangements, one of our personnel from the communications centre entered the room and spoke with Ambassador Thebault to report an incident at the Kaonik road junction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Described in terms as?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: To the effect that a 40-vehicle humanitarian convoy moving from Travnik to Zenica had been hijacked at the Busovaca junction by HVO troops and that the two escorting UNPROFOR Warrior vehicles had been separated from the humanitarian convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move on with what happened, and just again for setting, is this an interference with a convoy that led to any firing of guns and so on and any loss of life, or was this eventually one that was dealt with in some other way?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: It had the potential to deteriorate but fortunately was resolved without the use of force by either side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Incidents of this type, had you had dealings with incidents of this type before?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: Yes, I had. It was not unusual for convoys moving through Bosnia-Herzegovina to be stopped by one party or another, for one reason or another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the stopping of a convoy in itself necessarily amount to a breach of the agreements that had been hammered out with Halilovic, Petkovic, and others, or not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: Part of the agreement between the two parties had been for complete freedom of movement. It would have been understood that the humanitarian convoy, run by UNHCR, should have been free of arms and explosives and therefore there would have been no necessity for it to have been stopped again by either party en route, as long as it was escorted by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the past when you'd had to deal with this sort of problem, if you had, to whom had you turned?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: To the control mechanism operated by either side. Normally from the Croat point of view, we would have referred to the person responsible in Mostar for humanitarian relief and refugees, a Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we see that your note goes on to say something about no longer taking orders. Tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: The incident of breach of agreement for freedom of movement was a blatant breach of the understanding between the two parties, and as the two Generals had toured parts of Bosnia, Central Bosnia and Herzegovina, for the purpose of explaining the need for freedom of movement and ceasefire between the two parties, such an incident was inevitably a block and an obstacle to further peace in the region. And, therefore, although it was not in itself a breach of the agreement, specifically it was an instant that had to be overcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your note reads, "No longer taking orders from." Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: Ambassador Thebault, seeing that something was required to be done, asked General Petkovic to accompany him to the communications centre, saying that this was an ideal opportunity for the two parties to work together, to overcome obstacles. If the joint headquarters proposed was to be successful, they had to take action, and take action rapidly. So Ambassador Thebault and General Petkovic, followed by myself, moved to the communication centre. The idea being, that General Petkovic would telephone the necessary party to obtain the release of the convoy. In this case, the party concerned was considered to be Mr. Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pausing a minute. How many telephone calls, if more than one, were there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: Two telephone calls were made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what language did Petkovic speak?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the services of an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the interpreter translate what was said in the telephone calls?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: On completion of each call, the interpreter briefed Ambassador Thebault and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's that detail that you can tell us about?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then please tell us what happened in the first phone call, and then the second.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER DAVID BEESE
utterances.text: In the first phone call, General Petkovic spoke to Mr. Dario Kordic and instructed him to release the convoy. The reply was something to the effect that Mr. Kordic was not beholden to General Petkovic, was not obliged to follow his orders, any more than he was to Colonel Blaskic, and that he would not release the convoy. General Petkovic reported that to Ambassador Thebault, who advised him that, in the spirit of the agreements, that was not really satisfactory, and considering that the British Battalion had advised it would move the necessary strength to gain the release of a convoy, one way or the other, by force if necessary, Ambassador Thebault advised General Petkovic he should try again. General Petkovic phoned Mr. Kordic again, and on the second occasion it is understood that he advised Mr. Kordic that, for his own sake, and the safety of his men, he should release the convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
